headline: The US 10 year Treasury yield jumped to 5.114 percent, its highest since 2007, after September flash PMI showed the fastest private sector growth in more than five years, knocking the S&P 500 down 0.76 percent and lifting October Fed hike odds to about two thirds.

summary.us: The S&P 500 fell 0.76 percent to 7,706.03, the Nasdaq Composite lost 0.69 percent to 26,936.04 and the Dow dropped 1.03 percent to 51,511.59 on 23 September as the 10 year Treasury yield rose about 15 basis points to 5.114 percent, the highest since 2007, on hot S&P Global flash PMI data and hawkish remarks from Fed officials including Musalem and Goolsbee. CME FedWatch odds of an October hike moved to roughly two thirds from 55 percent a day earlier, the Russell 2000 fell 1.28 percent, and single stock moves were driven by company events rather than the tape: McDonald's fell on an investor day that pushed its 50,000 restaurant target to 2028, while CrowdStrike hit a 52 week high on target raises from Morgan Stanley and Stephens.
summary.india: The Nifty 50 closed at 23,446.80 on 23 September, up 117.80 points or 0.50 percent, and the Sensex added 299.17 points to 74,828.25, with the Nifty Metal index up about 2.2 percent on copper strength and a flagged government incentive scheme for domestic lithium and nickel, while Nifty IT fell about 1 percent. Bank Nifty ended at 56,548.90 and the PSU bank index rose about 1.15 percent; Bajaj Finance was the top Nifty gainer at 3.41 percent after UBS upgraded it to neutral and raised its target to Rs 1,100, and the rupee eased to about 95.71 per dollar on broad dollar strength. Note that the dashboard's one day change for the Nifty and Bank Nifty understates the session because the price feed has no 22 September bar.
summary.global: Tokyo reopened on 24 September after the five day Silver Week break and the Nikkei 225 traded up 1.73 percent to 66,146, while the Hang Seng slipped again to 24,730 and Europe finished narrowly mixed on 23 September with the DAX down 0.64 percent and the FTSE 100 down 0.31 percent. Crude snapped a five day losing run after Iran's president told the UN General Assembly that Iran would not surrender, with CNBC reporting Brent up 3.9 percent at 103.08 dollars and WTI up 1.8 percent at 92.16 dollars, although the dashboard's front month WTI line reads 91.56 dollars after the October contract rolled off; gold fell 1.08 percent and silver 2.01 percent as the dollar index rose 0.70 percent.

weekly.narrative: The week belonged to central banks. The Federal Reserve raised rates a quarter point on 16 September to 3.75 to 4 percent, its first hike since 2023, and the Bank of Japan followed on 18 September with a split 7 to 2 vote that lifted its policy rate to a 31 year high of 1.25 percent, yet the yen weakened past 156 per dollar because two board members dissented and Governor Ueda made no commitment to further moves. US equities finished mixed as the 10 year Treasury yield came back to about 5 percent after touching a 19 year high above 5.04 percent ahead of the Fed, with the Dow down 1.69 percent on the week while the Nasdaq Composite added 0.72 percent. India was the weak spot, where the Nifty and Sensex logged a sixth consecutive weekly decline, the longest losing run in six years, under crude above 100 dollars, tighter global policy and a deepening Tata Sons governance dispute. Metals held their ground, with copper up about 2 percent on the week as the Yangshan import premium climbed 72 percent in September to a near four year high and silver adding 3.46 percent, while crypto turned sharply higher into the weekend on post Fed relief and rotation into altcoins. Next week brings S&P Global flash PMIs on 23 September, a heavy run of Fed speakers, Costco and Nike earnings on 24 September, and in India the Varmora Granito, Elevate Campuses, ArMee Infotech and A-One Steels offers alongside the close of the NSE IPO on 21 September.
